title: When the Cipher Wakes
premise: True-crime podcaster Kestrel Iversen built her reputation closing cold cases no one else would touch, but the 1994 disappearance of her own mother was the one she swore never to investigate. When a confession letter arrives postmarked the day after her grandmother's funeral, Kestrel learns the case was buried inside her own family: her grandmother orchestrated the disappearance to protect a child born of an affair, and the letter's writer—an accomplice now dying—wants the truth surfaced before the last witness dies. As Kestrel peels back thirty-year-old alibis, she discovers her mother may still be alive, living under a borrowed identity and complicit in her own erasure. The novel ends with Kestrel choosing to broadcast the truth, sacrificing her career's perfect record to give her mother back her real name.
about_author: Yara Almeida is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unsolved case files in coastal New England before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about families that keep their secrets too well.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Kestrel Iversen, POV. Days after her grandmother Edith's funeral, a confession letter arrives claiming responsibility for a 1994 disappearance. Kestrel recognizes the missing woman's name before she's ready to: it belongs on her own family tree. The emotional beat is dread dressed as professional curiosity—the case she built a career avoiding has just knocked on her door.

chapters.title: The Case She Never Took
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV, in flashback and present. We learn her rules: no family cases, no unsolvable timelines. Her producer Marcus pushes her to ignore the letter; her listener base is already speculating. Kestrel rereads the letter and finds a detail only someone at the scene could know. Emotional beat: the crack in her armor—she can't un-know what she knows.

chapters.title: Saltwater Records
chapters.summary: Kestrel travels to Grayhaven, the coastal town her mother fled from. At the county archives she pulls the original file and finds pages missing—torn cleanly, deliberately. The archivist, an old classmate named Ruth, remembers Edith visiting the same file years ago. Emotional beat: the vertigo of realizing her grandmother got here first.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibi
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. She reconstructs the official timeline: her mother Lark vanished from a ferry dock; Edith's brother Hal had the only verified sighting. Interviewing the now-elderly Hal, Kestrel catches him rehearsing his answer. Emotional beat: cold clarity—everyone who testified in 1994 is still protecting the same story.

chapters.title: The Dying Accomplice
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV, tracing the letter. The postmark leads to a hospice in Portsmouth, where a former ferry clerk, Dennis Okafor, admits he mailed the letter for a friend. He won't name the friend, only says: 'She wanted it to come after the funeral, so Edith couldn't burn it.' Emotional beat: grief curdling into anger at the grandmother she mourned.

chapters.title: Edith's Boxes
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV, sorting Edith's estate. Behind a false drawer: Lark's birth certificate, a second passport, and thirty years of cash withdrawals in small, steady amounts. Someone has been paying for something—or someone—for decades. Emotional beat: betrayal braided with hope; the payments mean her mother might have been alive all along.

chapters.title: What the Ferryman Saw
chapters.summary: Hal's POV. 1994 flashback: Hal saw Lark at the dock with a suitcase and a man, and she asked him to lie—not for herself, but because 'Edith will lose everything otherwise.' Present-day Hal, dying of guilt, decides to tell Kestrel the truth he's carried. Emotional beat: the weight of a kept promise finally cracking.

chapters.title: The Man on the Dock
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Hal's deathbed confession names the man: Tomas Reyes, a fisherman who left Grayhaven the same week Lark did. Kestrel finds his obituary—three years old—and a surviving daughter in Providence. Emotional beat: the thrill of a live thread after decades of cold ends.

chapters.title: Daughter of the Fisherman
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV, meeting Lucia Reyes, who grew up believing her father was a widower. Lucia shares photos: a woman in the background of a 1998 birthday party whose face stops Kestrel cold. Emotional beat: recognition and terror in the same breath—the woman is Lark, aged twenty years.

chapters.title: The Second Name
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV, working the alias from the second passport: 'Marin Vale.' She finds a quiet paper trail—a teaching license, a library card, a small house in Vermont. Someone has lived a careful, deliberate life. Emotional beat: awe at the discipline of erasure, and fear of what confronting it might destroy.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Back at the studio, someone has accessed Kestrel's research drive; episode drafts are deleted. Marcus suspects a listener, but the login traces to Grayhaven's municipal network. Emotional beat: paranoia—the case is pushing back, and someone local is still invested in the old story staying dead.

chapters.title: The Town That Agreed
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. She canvasses Grayhaven elders and finds the same phrase repeated verbatim in different mouths: 'Lark ran off.' Ruth admits the town's leading families coordinated the story in 1994—Edith asked, and they obeyed, because Edith knew things about all of them. Emotional beat: horror at how easily a whole town became an accomplice.

chapters.title: Edith's Ledger
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. In Edith's effects she finds a coded ledger—her grandmother's lifelong habit of cipher. Decoded, it lists payments to 'M.V.' alongside hush sums to five town families, and one final entry, dated the week of the funeral: 'Tell her everything. She deserves the choice.' Emotional beat: reluctant tenderness—Edith's control was also, twistedly, protection.

chapters.title: The Fifth Family
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Four of the five hush-sum families are accounted for. The fifth is the Calloways, whose patriarch was the harbor commissioner in 1994—and whose grandson now sits on the town council and has been asking Ruth about Kestrel's visits. Emotional beat: the case acquires a living antagonist with everything to lose.

chapters.title: Break-In
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, night scene. Someone ransacks her rental cottage, taking the ledger but missing the photocopies hidden in her car. A councilman's truck idles at the end of the lane. Kestrel records everything and sends it to Marcus as insurance. Emotional beat: fear sharpened into defiance—she's no longer investigating; she's at war.

chapters.title: What Lark Chose
chapters.summary: Marin Vale's POV, unnamed at first. A Vermont schoolteacher with careful routines reads a news alert about a podcaster digging in Grayhaven. We learn her daily rituals of vigilance and the ache of watching her daughter's career from a distance she chose. Emotional beat: the cost of survival—she has been free for thirty years and never once at peace.

chapters.title: The Calloway Version
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV, confronting the young councilman, Daniel Calloway, who claims his grandfather merely 'helped a scared woman leave.' But Kestrel's decoded ledger shows the Calloway payment doubled after 1996—the year Tomas Reyes died suspiciously in a boating accident. Emotional beat: the mystery deepens from concealment to possible murder.

chapters.title: Reyes's Last Voyage
chapters.summary: Lucia's POV. Lucia, spurred by Kestrel's questions, reopens her father's accident file and finds the Coast Guard report contradicts the official story: the boat's bilge was tampered with. She sends Kestrel the file. Emotional beat: two daughters of buried truths converging—grief becoming purpose.

chapters.title: The Broadcast Decision
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Marcus warns that airing unverified murder allegations will end her career and expose 'Marin Vale' to danger. Kestrel realizes she's been protecting the perfect record, not her mother. She drafts the final episode: every document, every name, including her own family's guilt. Emotional beat: surrender of identity—the investigator who closes cases chooses truth over winning.

chapters.title: Vermont, Unannounced
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, climax part one. Kestrel drives to the Vermont house and knocks. A gray-haired woman opens the door, and the episode between them—rage, grief, thirty years of silence—unfolds in a kitchen. Lark admits she witnessed the Calloway patriarch's crime in 1994 and fled with Edith's help; Tomas found her years later and was silenced for it. Emotional beat: the raw collision of daughter and mother across a gulf of chosen absence.

chapters.title: The Last Episode
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, climax part two. The Calloways move to suppress the broadcast with legal threats and a break-in at the studio; Marcus airs it anyway from a backup feed. The episode detonates: the state reopens the Reyes case, Daniel Calloway resigns, and Grayhaven's coordinated lie becomes national news. Emotional beat: catharsis—the truth landing like a wave that was always coming.

chapters.title: A Name Returned
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Lark, alternating POV, epilogue. Months later, Lark legally reclaims her name; the two navigate a fragile, honest relationship—no promises of closeness, only of truth. Kestrel launches a new series about cases the system buried willingly, her perfect record happily broken. Final beat: identity as inheritance—what we keep, what we choose, what we finally say out loud.
